messages.subject: Convergence issues with the spatial covariance parameters
messages.subject_clean: Convergence issues with the spatial covariance parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hello there,

I am fitting a single-season spatial occupancy model (`spPGOcc`) for a rare species. My dataset includes more than 1,000 camera-trap sites, but the species was detected at only 78 sites. I modelled detection separately, then compared the matched spatial and non-spatial occupancy models.

The spatial model had a slightly lower WAIC than the non-spatial model, but the difference was small (ΔWAIC < 2). The non-spatial model converged well; however, residual diagnostics indicated positive short-distance spatial autocorrelation. I therefore explored spatial models using an NNGP with 15 neighbours and several plausible priors on the spatial effective range (e.g., 3–30 km and 5–50 km), with longer MCMC runs.

The regression coefficients are generally stable and converge well across these fits. However, the spatial covariance parameters, especially `sigma.sq` and sometimes `phi`, remain difficult to converge and have low ESS. In some fits, the posterior for `phi` also approaches the lower prior bound, suggesting support for a longer effective range than allowed by the prior.

What would be the most appropriate next step? Further increasing the number of MCMC iterations, using more informative priors on `phi` and/or `sigma.sq`, changing the NNGP neighbour specification, or treating the spatial model primarily as a sensitivity analysis while focusing inference on covariate estimates that are stable across priors?

Thanks

Best,
Tashi

messages.subject: Re: Convergence issues with the spatial covariance parameters
messages.subject_clean: Convergence issues with the spatial covariance parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tashi,

Thanks for the message. Your model output from spPGOcc that you shared suggests quite strong convergence of all parameters. It is to be expected that the ESS values will be lower for sigma.sq and phi as they almost always will mix more slowly than other parameters in a spatial occupancy model. This is in part due to the fact that there is statistical theory showing that the two parameters cannot be separately identified from one another and rather it is their product that is truly identifiable. This, and other convergence considerations for spatial occupancy models, are described in this vignette here <https://doserlab.com/files/spoccupancy-web/articles/modelconsiderations>.

With all that said, if delta WAIC is less than 2 between the spatial and nonspatial model, I would suggest using the nonspatial model unless you have a strong reason to not do so. With a WAIC that is that much smaller, it indicates little performance benefits of the spatial model relative to the nonspatial model, and so you would prefer to use the simpler, nonspatial model. You could also run some cross-validation to get an additional assessment of whether the spatial model provides any improvements to the nonspatial model. If you are really worried about residual spatial autocorrelation, then you could also use the residuals() function with the output from the PGOcc() model to determine if there are any indications of residual spatial autocorrelation in the residuals of the nonspatial model.

Hope that helps,

Jeff

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your response Jeff!
I appreciate your input and apologies about the late response.
I was actually wrong about my simpler models appearing to converge for RE, this was actually only true with a stricter prior on sigma.sp.psi. For the species of salamander in question my detections are as you described, "small number of detections...highly clustered in a small set of sites". So I think my data just doesn't support estimation of this parameter as you said. In a situation such as this, would you suggest dropping the RE all together and treating all my reaches as independent rather than nesting them within sites or just acknowledging the issues I had with estimation of RE but maintaining the the random intercept to reflect the nested nature of my design?

Best,

Jacob

On Tue, Jul 28, 2026 at 9:42 PM Jeffrey Doser <jwd...@ncsu.edu> wrote:
> Hi Jacob,
>
> Thanks for the question. This problem could arise for a variety of reasons. First off, it certainly seems like the random effect variance is unidentifiable in this case given the massive credible interval. This could be a result of the data for this species not being able to estimate all parameters in this model (e.g., if there are a small number of detections, the detections are highly clustered in a small set of the sites). I would not recommend simply trying to set a stricter prior on sigma.sq.psi, as this suggests to me there is not enough data to identify the problem. I would encourage you to take a look at the traceplots of the random effect estimates (i.e., both the variance in "sigma.sq.psi.samples" as well as the actual estimated random effect intercepts stored in beta.star.samples). Looking at those values may help reveal the root cause of what's causing the problems with estimating the random effect. In your simpler models that you say converge, I would also look at the magnitude of the credible intervals for the variance. Is it similarly large, or are the values more reasonable? If they are more reasonable, this likely indicates the full model is too complex and the data for the species can't estimate the parameters. If it is similarly large, the model still may just not have much information to estimate the random effect. Regardless, I'd encourage you to dig into the actual locations of where the detections for this species are and how that might be contributing to the challenge in estimating the RE variances.
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> Jeff

messages.subject_clean: [External] Re: Convergence issues of occurrence random effect variance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jacob,

In an ideal world, you'd be able to account for the nested design with inclusion of the RE to properly account for the non-independence between reaches in a site. The approaches you mention both have their pros and cons. If you drop the RE, then you have to recognize that you'll be ignoring some dependencies in your data and thus your credible intervals will be overly precise (e.g., should actually be wider than what they are), so you'd need to be cautious in your interpretation of "significant" effects. Alternatively, if you decide to use the RE, I would not recommend just using the default prior with non-converged results, but rather use some form of more constrained prior (e..g, you could use a uniform prior instead of an IG prior). You would need to make this abundantly clear when you describe the model that you are restricting the prior in order to accommodate the dependency structure in the data set while still ensuring convergence.

Alternatively, it seems like you're working with multiple species here, so you could also explore the use of a multi-species model, which often can improve estimation of these types of random effects by sharing across species.

Hope that helps,

Jeff

This makes my options more clear. Best,
Jacob

You would need to make this abundantly clear when you describe the model that you are restricting the prior in order to accommodate the dependency structure in the data set while still ensuring convergence.
> >
> > Alternatively, it seems like you're working with multiple species here, so you could also explore the use of a multi-species model, which often can improve estimation of these types of random effects by sharing across species.
> >
> > Hope that helps,

This could be a result of the data for this species not being able to estimate all parameters in this model (e.g., if there are a small number of detections, the detections are highly clustered in a small set of the sites). I would not recommend simply trying to set a stricter prior on sigma.sq.psi, as this suggests to me there is not enough data to identify the problem. I would encourage you to take a look at the traceplots of the random effect estimates (i.e., both the variance in "sigma.sq.psi.samples" as well as the actual estimated random effect intercepts stored in beta.star.samples). Looking at those values may help reveal the root cause of what's causing the problems with estimating the random effect. In your simpler models that you say converge, I would also look at the magnitude of the credible intervals for the variance. Is it similarly large, or are the values more reasonable? If they are more reasonable, this likely indicates the full model is too complex and the data for the species can't estimate the parameters. If it is similarly large, the model still may just not have much information to estimate the random effect. Regardless, I'd encourage you to dig into the actual locations of where the detections for this species are and how that might be contributing to the challenge in estimating the RE variances.
